title: The DNA Feature's Nearest Neuron
takeaway: The neuron that comes closest to the DNA feature is not a DNA neuron: across its whole activation range, and in random examples drawn from the top of that range, the DNA proxy fires on only a thin sliver of tokens and no nucleotide strings appear. The paper reads this as evidence that dictionary learning found something the neuron basis does not already contain, rather than relabelling an already-clean neuron.
walkthrough:
**What this is.** A histogram of one neuron's activations, drawn in the same format the paper uses for its learned features ([[feature-activation-distribution-plot]]). The title names the unit: A/neurons/67. Under the paper's [[neuron-notation]], "A/neurons/" marks an MLP neuron of transformer A — one of the 512 in the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]] — not one of the 4,096 dictionary entries in run A/1.

**Why a neuron is on the page.** The [[dna-feature]] A/1/2937 fires on long uppercase runs of A, T, C and G. Before crediting dictionary learning with finding it, the paper checks whether the feature is just a neuron under a new name ([[feature-neuron-nonalignment]]). One route in is the [[most-correlated-neuron]]: the neuron whose activations track the feature's most closely over roughly 40 million dataset examples. For A/1/2937 that neuron is A/neurons/67.

**How to read it.** Left to right is the neuron's activation on a token, from just above zero out to about 6.4. Exact zeros are pulled out to the two ticks at the far left, because sparsity would otherwise put a spike at 0. Height is how many tokens land at that activation.

Color is not activation. It is the [[dna-proxy]], the [[computational-proxy]] score $\log(P(s|\text{DNA})/P(s))$ ([[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]]). Red means the string is far likelier under a DNA model than under ordinary text; blue means it is not. The band underneath renormalizes each column to full height, so even a small red fraction stays visible.

The four boxes hold random dataset examples at the four activation levels the dotted lines mark. Each line is one sampled token, bolded, with four tokens of context on either side; orange shading tracks how hard the neuron fires there.

**What it shows.** Blue, all the way across. The red sliver along the bottom never grows into a majority, even at the neuron's highest activations. The top box, near activation 6.2, holds GDHVRSKVFKQEKGKE and TTSAVAAQRGYST — protein-style letter runs — plus FIS3, SPSS and TRY_RUN. Capital letters of many kinds, no nucleotide strings. That mixture is ordinary [[polysemanticity]], the condition [[superposition]] predicts.

The feature's own version of this plot peaks near 23K tokens and reaches activation 11.4, going mostly red at the top. This neuron peaks near 0.8M, about thirty-five times denser.

**One caveat about the pointer.** The sentence introducing this item names a different neuron, A/neurons/227 — the one with the largest [[neuron-basis-coefficients]] in the feature's direction vector — and makes the same claim about it. The panel printed here is the correlation check, not the coefficient one, and the paper prints no numeric value for that coefficient. It says elsewhere that it trusts the correlation route more, since neurons differ in activation scale.

terms.definition: The plot's title and its type: a histogram over tokens of how strongly one unit fires, with dataset examples pinned above chosen activation levels. Here it is applied to a neuron rather than to a learned feature.
The unit plotted: neuron 67 of the 512-neuron MLP in transformer A. It is here because its activations correlate more strongly with the DNA feature's than any other neuron's.

A different neuron, named in the sentence that introduces this item: the one with the largest coefficient in the DNA feature's dictionary vector. The paper says it too has no DNA in its top activating examples; it is not the neuron drawn here.
The DNA feature this whole check is about: feature 2937 of the 4,096 learned in dictionary run A/1 on transformer A. It fires on long uppercase strings of A, T, C and G.
The paper's way of writing a transformer MLP neuron, as against the run/size/index form used for learned features. It keeps the two kinds of unit distinguishable in a sentence.
The label on the row of four boxes: text snippets sampled from the corpus at the activation levels the dotted lines mark, showing what the neuron actually fires on there.
How many tokens in the visualization sample fall at each activation level. It is a count, not a probability, and it excludes the tokens where the neuron is exactly off.
The scalar post-ReLU value of the neuron on a token. Higher means the neuron fires harder on that token.

The quantity the colors encode: how much likelier the surrounding string is under a DNA model than under a general text model. It is the paper's independent yardstick, computed without reference to the model.
The concrete score used here, $\log(P(s|\text{DNA})/P(s))$, with DNA modelled as a random string over the characters A, T, C and G and evaluated on groups of at least two tokens.
The paper's general device: a cheap, hand-built score for "is this the hypothesized context", used to test a unit's interpretation instead of trusting eyeballed examples.
Reads the color bar's direction: moving right along the bar, toward red, means more DNA-like. Blue is the other end.
The continuous scale mapping proxy values onto the filled area of the histogram. It is not binarized here, unlike the version of this plot used for the feature's specificity check.

terms.term: Renormalized band (the strip below the histogram)
terms.definition: The same red/blue split with each activation column stretched to full height, so proportions can be read where the raw density is nearly flat. It is what makes the thin DNA fraction at high activations visible at all.

terms.term: 0 and >0 ticks (far left of the axis)
terms.definition: Markers separating tokens where the neuron is exactly off from tokens where it is on. Zeros are held out of the density because sparsity would otherwise put a spike at the origin.
Vertical lines connecting each example box down to the activation level its snippets were sampled from.
Inside the example boxes, how strongly the neuron fires on each token; darker orange is a stronger activation, no shading is off.
The token each example line is centered on — the one the sample was drawn for. The four tokens on either side are context.
A run of the letters A, T, C and G representing DNA, such as AGTTTCGTTTAC. The claim of this item is that none appear among this neuron's top examples.
An entry of a feature's direction vector, which lives in the 512-dimensional space of MLP neurons. Its size says how much that one neuron contributes to the feature's direction.

terms.term: The feature is not a neuron
terms.definition: The check this item belongs to: showing that dictionary learning did not simply hand back a neuron that was already clean, since that would make the result trivial.
One unit responding to a mixture of unrelated inputs. The mixture of protein fragments, acronyms and code identifiers in the top box is what it looks like here.
The hypothesis that the model packs more features than it has neurons by giving each a direction spread across many neurons, which is why a feature can have no neuron of its own.

numbers.meaning: The index of the plotted neuron among the MLP's 512. It was picked not by hand but by search: it is the neuron whose activations correlate most with the DNA feature's.

The index of the neuron named in the introducing sentence, selected by a different criterion — the largest coefficient in the DNA feature's dictionary vector. The paper makes the same negative claim about it but prints no plot of it here and no value for that coefficient.
The DNA feature's index within run A/1. Feature indices carry no order or meaning; they are just slots in the dictionary.
The width of the MLP layer being decomposed, and so the number of neurons any such comparison can draw from. It is also the dimension of the vector whose coefficients pick out A/neurons/227.
The number of features in run A/1, the dictionary the paper analyses in detail. It is 8 times 512, the expansion factor chosen so the dictionary can hold more features than the layer has neurons.
The expansion factor of run A/1: features per neuron. The paper trains dictionaries from 1x up to 256x, but focuses its detailed work on this one.
The span of the x-axis: the neuron's activation range over the visualization sample. The right edge is roughly where its largest observed activation falls.
The x-axis ticks. They are plain activation units with no normalization, so they are comparable only within this one unit — a neuron's scale need not match a feature's.
The y-axis ticks, in millions of tokens. The curve peaks just under 0.8M immediately above zero activation, meaning the great majority of the neuron's firing is weak.

numbers.value: 23K (peak of the feature's own version of this plot)
numbers.meaning: For comparison: the DNA feature's activation distribution peaks near 23 thousand tokens where this neuron peaks near 800 thousand. The neuron is roughly thirty-five times denser, which is the ordinary situation — features are sparse by construction, neurons are not.
The DNA feature runs to roughly activation 11.4, and its high end turns mostly red. That contrast is the point of putting the two plots near each other.

The color bar's ticks, in log units of the likelihood ratio. Zero is the break-even point where the string is equally likely as DNA or as ordinary text; +5 means about 148 times likelier as DNA, -5 about 148 times less likely.

The four activation levels the dotted lines mark, and so the levels the example boxes sample from. They are spread across the range, with the last near the top, so the reader can see whether purity improves as the neuron fires harder.

numbers.value: 5 lines per box, 20 examples in total
numbers.meaning: How many random snippets are shown at each level. It is a small sample, which is why the paper also reports the full colored distribution rather than resting on the boxes alone.
The window drawn around each sampled token, per the paper's activation-visualization appendix. It is narrow, so a long DNA run would still be recognizable but a long-range context cue might not be.
The size of the training-data subset used to build these visualizations, taking only 10 tokens from each context so the sample spans many documents.
The number of examples over which the feature-to-neuron activation correlation was computed to select A/neurons/67. A large sample matters because both units are off on most tokens.

The Pearson correlation between the binarized DNA proxy and the DNA feature's activations, reported one section earlier. It is the number this neuron's picture is implicitly measured against: the feature tracks the proxy, the neuron does not.

From the parallel Arabic case, the only place the paper prints coefficient magnitudes: 27 neurons had coefficients of at least 0.1 in that feature's direction, and the three largest were negative. It is offered as the shape of what a top coefficient means — one entry among many, not a stand-in for the feature.
